topics.title: The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill falls one vote-share short of women's reservation
topics.hook: On 17 April 2026 the Lok Sabha voted 298 to 230 for a bill meant to fast-track women's reservation and expand the House to 850 seats, and the bill still failed, because a constitutional amendment needs two-thirds of members present and voting, not a simple majority.
topics.story:
Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal introduced the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 in the Lok Sabha on 16 April. Twenty-four hours later it was dead. The vote was 298 in favour and 230 against, out of 528 members present. That looks like a win by any ordinary counting. It was not. Article 368 requires certain amendments to clear a majority of the total membership of the House and two-thirds of members present and voting. Two-thirds of 528 is 352. The bill fell 54 votes short.

The bill's real purpose was to unstick the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023, the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, which had already reserved one-third of Lok Sabha and state assembly seats for women — on paper. That reservation was written to activate only after delimitation following \"the first census taken after 2026,\" a phrase inserted by the 84th and 87th Amendments in 2001 and 2003 to extend a freeze on seat numbers first imposed by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. Since 1976, Lok Sabha seats have stayed fixed at 1971 Census levels regardless of how unevenly India's population has actually grown since. Waiting for a full delimitation cycle after the 2026 Census could have pushed the women's quota out to the 2030s.

The 131st Amendment tried to route around that wait. It proposed using 2011 Census data instead of the still-incomplete 2026 Census, and it proposed expanding the Lok Sabha from 543 elected seats to 850 — 815 from states, 35 from Union Territories — the first size increase since 1976. Two dependent bills rode on its success: the Delimitation Bill, 2026, which would have redrawn constituency boundaries, and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, which extended the same logic to UT legislatures.

The opposition came from an unlikely direction: not from parties opposed to women's reservation, but from states that had succeeded at population control. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Odisha stood to lose relative seat share under any population-based formula, because their fertility rates fell decades before the northern Hindi belt's did. Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, which grew faster, stood to gain. Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M.K. Stalin called the bill a \"historic injustice\" that would punish states for succeeding at development, and organised black-flag protests on 16 April, the day the bill was tabled.

When the amendment failed, both dependent bills were withdrawn the same day. The 106th Amendment remains law, technically in force, still waiting for the delimitation exercise it was never given the numbers to survive.

For an exam, this episode is really two questions wearing one costume. One is procedural: what makes an amendment a \"special majority\" amendment, and how do you compute whether 298 for and 230 against passes or fails. The other is substantive: which amendment did what, since the 106th (already law) and the 131st (which failed) are easy to mix up in a rushed reading. A good passage would give you the raw vote numbers and ask you to work out the outcome yourself, or would ask which amendment actually reserved the seats versus which one tried, and failed, to make that reservation usable sooner.

topics.title: Tamil Nadu gets its first hung assembly, and a film star's party tops the poll
topics.hook: Tamil Nadu voted on 23 April 2026 with the highest turnout in its history, and for the first time since 1967 no single Dravidian bloc came out with a majority — a two-year-old party founded by actor Vijay finished on top with 108 seats, twelve short of the 118 needed to govern alone.
topics.story:
Tamil Nadu has been governed by one of two Dravidian parties, the DMK or the AIADMK, in every election since 1967. That fifty-nine-year pattern broke on 23 April 2026. Polling for all 234 seats happened in a single phase and recorded 85.1 percent turnout, the highest the state has ever logged. When results came on 4 May, Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam, the party actor Thalapathy Vijay launched in 2024, emerged as the single largest party with 108 seats — more than either Dravidian giant, but short of the 118-seat majority mark.

The DMK-led Secular Progressive Alliance, which had governed since 2021 under Chief Minister M.K. Stalin, was reduced to 73 seats: 59 for the DMK itself and 5 for the Congress, the rest split among smaller allies. The AIADMK-led NDA alliance did worse still, taking 53 seats, of which the AIADMK held 47 and the BJP, contesting a state where it has never won more than a handful of seats, took just one. No combination reaches 118 without TVK, which suddenly holds the balance of power in a state assembly for the first time in the Dravidian era.

Vijay built TVK on a platform against what he called \"family rule\" in both established parties, drawing on decades of fan-club infrastructure built through his film career the way MGR and Jayalalithaa once did before him. His campaign avoided allying formally with either the DMK-led or AIADMK-led blocs, betting that Tamil Nadu voters wanted a third option untethered to either dynasty. The bet worked well enough to make TVK the single largest party, but not well enough to let it govern without help.

A hung assembly forces a governor's call on who gets first chance to prove a majority, and it opens the door to horse-trading, defections and possibly another election if no coalition holds. Tamil Nadu's Raj Bhavan and its 234 MLAs now sit at the centre of a genuinely new kind of Tamil political arithmetic — one built around a third force rather than the DMK-AIADMK binary that has organised the state since the death of C.N. Annadurai.

For CLAT, this is the year's cleanest example of anti-defection law and coalition mechanics colliding with a real electoral map. Expect questions on the Tenth Schedule, on what a governor is constitutionally required to do when no party has a majority, and on how a hung assembly differs from a coalition government formed after a pre-poll alliance. It is also a rare, current, testable instance of a film star converting box-office fame into first-past-the-post seats at genuinely disruptive scale, worth comparing with MGR's AIADMK founding in 1972 and NTR's Telugu Desam Party in 1982.

topics.title: West Bengal votes out Mamata Banerjee's fifteen-year government
topics.hook: West Bengal voted in two phases, on 23 and 29 April 2026, and the BJP won 206 of the state's 293 assembly seats, ending Mamata Banerjee's Trinamool Congress government after fifteen unbroken years in power.
topics.story:
Mamata Banerjee took Bengal from the Left Front's thirty-four-year rule in 2011 and had governed continuously since, surviving a hard-fought 2021 election that the BJP entered expecting to win. Five years later, the result reversed. Voting was split into two phases to manage the state's size and its history of poll violence: the first phase on 23 April covered 152 constituencies, the second on 29 April covered the remaining 142 (out of 294 total, minus one seat, Falta, that did not go to polls that cycle). Counting on 4 May gave the BJP 206 seats against Trinamool's fraction of that tally, a scale of defeat few pollsters had forecast even a month earlier.

Banerjee herself filed her nomination from her long-held seat of Bhabanipur on 8 April, a signal that the party still expected to contest from strength. The result instead handed the BJP a majority that lets it form government without needing allies, the first time the party has governed Bengal on its own since the state's creation. Suvendu Adhikari, a former Trinamool minister who defected to the BJP before the 2021 election and became Leader of the Opposition after that loss, becomes central to how the new government is read: his defection, which barely dented Trinamool five years ago, now looks like the opening move in a longer campaign that finally paid off.

The defeat matters beyond Bengal's borders because Trinamool has been one of the more durable regional counterweights to the BJP in eastern India, and its removal changes the arithmetic of opposition unity at the national level heading into the next Lok Sabha cycle. It also lands amid an ongoing Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls that has been contentious in Bengal specifically, given the state's history of disputes over migrant and refugee voter status along the Bangladesh border.

A CLAT passage on this result would likely test the mechanics of multi-phase elections under the Election Commission's Model Code of Conduct, the constitutional position of a Chief Minister once an assembly's term effectively ends with a change of government, and comparative federalism: how the loss of a major state changes the composition of bodies like the Rajya Sabha and the GST Council, both of which are shaped by which parties hold which state governments.

topics.title: Fifty-one countries meet on the Strait of Hormuz as the 2026 Iran war grinds on
topics.hook: France and the United Kingdom co-chaired a summit of 51 countries on 17 April 2026 to defend freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint carrying roughly a fifth of the world's traded oil, five weeks into a war that began when the US and Israel killed Iran's supreme leader.
topics.story:
The war that produced this summit began on 28 February 2026, when the United States and Israel launched air strikes on Iran and killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran retaliated with missile and drone attacks on Israel, on US bases across the Gulf, and on US-allied Gulf states; its Revolutionary Guard Corps then moved to choke the Strait of Hormuz itself, boarding merchant ships, laying sea mines, and warning that passage through the strait would not be guaranteed. A ceasefire negotiated by American and Iranian negotiators held from early April for roughly sixty days before collapsing in mid-June and then again in July, after Iran struck three commercial vessels that had bypassed its preapproved shipping route.

Amid that fragile early-April lull, President Emmanuel Macron and Prime Minister Keir Starmer convened 51 countries in an International Summit on the Strait of Hormuz on 17 April, underlining what their joint statement called the international community's determination to support freedom of navigation, uphold international law, and protect global energy security. The choice of co-chairs was itself notable: neither France nor Britain is a Gulf littoral state, but both hold permanent UN Security Council seats and both have historically framed freedom-of-navigation disputes as matters for the wider international system rather than for regional actors alone.

The strait's geography explains why so many countries showed up. It separates Iran from Oman across a channel only 33 kilometres wide at its narrowest, with shipping lanes on each side just 3 kilometres across. Roughly a fifth of the world's oil, and a comparable share of global LNG exports from Qatar, passes through it, so a serious blockage does not stay a regional problem. India felt this directly: an Indian tanker, the Jag Vasant, sat stranded in the strait for 23 days before finally docking in Mumbai with an LPG cargo the government had been anxiously tracking against a possible domestic cooking-gas shortage. Iran also struck the United Arab Emirates directly in early April, and the UAE's air defences intercepted 19 ballistic missiles and 26 drones in a single wave, a scale of interception that says as much about the size of the attack as about Emirati air defence capability.

For India, the war forces an uncomfortable balancing act. New Delhi has deepened defence and energy ties with Israel and the Gulf Arab states over the past decade while also maintaining a long relationship with Iran, including investment in Chabahar port as an alternate route into Afghanistan and Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan. India's official position has been to express \"deep concern\" and urge restraint on all sides without naming an aggressor, a studiedly neutral formula that mirrors its historical non-alignment instinct more than any recent India foreign-policy statement on West Asia.

A CLAT passage on this would likely pair the geography (chokepoint economics, the 20-percent oil-flow figure) with international law (freedom of navigation under UNCLOS, the law of the sea on territorial straits) and with India's specific stakes (energy security, the stranded-tanker episode, Chabahar). It also invites comparison with older oil-shock precedents: the 1973 Arab oil embargo and the Iran-Iraq War's own Tanker War in the 1980s, both of which are standard static-GK reference points for chokepoint questions.

topics.title: India's first caste census since 1931 begins counting 1.4 billion people
topics.hook: India's 16th decennial census began houselisting operations on 1 April 2026, over three million officials deployed, and for the first time since 1931 it is collecting caste data — a question the government dropped from every census after Independence.
topics.story:
The census is India's largest single administrative exercise, and this one carries two firsts. It is the country's first fully digital census, run through a mobile app with real-time data upload, and it includes a self-enumeration window, from 1 to 15 April, letting citizens fill in their own household details online rather than waiting for an enumerator. It is also the first census since 1931 to collect caste data at the individual level; India recorded caste in every census under British rule but has not done so since 1951, when the newly independent government decided the practice risked entrenching social divisions rather than easing them.

The exercise runs in two phases. Houselisting and Housing Census operations, covering the physical count of households, dwellings, and basic amenities, began on 1 April 2026 and continue until 30 September 2026. The second phase, the Population Enumeration, is scheduled for February 2027 and will collect demographic detail: age, education, migration history, occupation and, this time, caste and sub-caste identity. Because the population count itself falls in the following year, the exercise is formally referred to by some official sources as the 2027 Census even though its first phase started in 2026.

The scale is difficult to overstate. More than 34 lakh personnel, including roughly 1.3 lakh census functionaries plus enumerators and supervisors, are being deployed to count an estimated 1.4 billion people. The total budgeted cost is about ₹11,718 crore, commonly rounded in reporting to roughly $1.24 billion, spent across a single continuous year-long field operation.

The caste question is where the exercise turns political rather than merely administrative. Comprehensive caste enumeration last happened under British rule in the 1931 Census; independent India's government dropped it in 1951, arguing that counting caste would calcify a hierarchy the Constitution was trying to dismantle. Every subsequent Mandal-era and post-Mandal debate over reservation quotas for Other Backward Classes has run on estimates and survey data rather than a hard census count, because no head-count of caste has existed for nearly a century. Supporters of this year's caste question argue that accurate numbers are overdue for evidence-based policy on reservation ceilings; critics, including some religious-minority advocacy groups, worry that formalising caste categories for Muslims and Christians, communities that do not always map neatly onto the Hindu caste framework used historically, could complicate rather than clarify questions of quota eligibility and even, some fear, citizenship documentation.

A CLAT reading-comprehension passage on this topic sits naturally alongside the 131st Amendment Bill, since both concern the same underlying tension: how you count a population, and what political consequences follow from the method you choose. Expect questions distinguishing the 1931 precedent from the 1951 policy reversal, testing the two-phase structure and its dates, and probing the reasoning on both sides of the caste-data debate rather than treating it as a settled question.

topics.title: A nine-judge bench reopens Sabarimala, and religious freedom for everyone with it
topics.hook: A nine-judge Supreme Court bench began sixteen days of hearings on 7 April 2026 to review the 2018 Sabarimala judgment, reopening not just the question of women's temple entry but the broader test courts use to decide which religious practices the Constitution actually protects.
topics.story:
In September 2018, a five-judge Constitution Bench ruled 4-1 that Sabarimala temple's practice of barring women aged 10 to 50 — broadly, those of menstruating age — from entering violated Articles 14, 15 and 25 of the Constitution. The ruling triggered mass protests in Kerala and dozens of review and curative petitions. Rather than deciding those petitions on the merits, the Court in 2020 referred a wider set of questions to a larger bench, reasoning that Sabarimala could not be resolved in isolation from similar disputes elsewhere: the entry of Muslim women into mosques and dargahs, the entry of Parsi women who marry outside the faith into fire temples, and the practice of female genital cutting among the Dawoodi Bohra community. Sixty-six separate matters now sit tagged to what is formally called the Sabarimala Reference.

The nine-judge bench, headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant, opened hearings on 7 April 2026. The schedule ran in stages: review petitioners and their supporting parties argued from 7 to 9 April; the original writ petitioners who oppose reopening the 2018 verdict argued from 14 to 16 April; rejoinders and amicus curiae submissions followed on 21 and 22 April. After sixteen days of hearings, the bench reserved judgment on 14 May 2026, meaning the ruling itself will land outside this month but the constitutional stakes were set within it.

What is actually being tested is not Sabarimala alone but the doctrine of Essential Religious Practices, the framework Indian courts have used since the 1954 Shirur Mutt case to decide which religious customs Article 25's freedom-of-religion guarantee actually protects. Under that doctrine, a court asks whether a practice is essential to a religion's core theology before deciding whether the state can interfere with it — a test critics have long argued turns judges into theologians. The bench is also weighing Article 26, which protects religious denominations' own right to manage their affairs, against the equality guarantees in Articles 14 and 15, and considering whether Sabarimala's Ayyappa devotees, who observe a vow of celibacy before pilgrimage, constitute a separate religious denomination with rights distinct from Hinduism generally.

The reference sits inside a longer Indian pattern: courts asked to referee where individual constitutional rights end and group religious autonomy begins, a tension that runs through the triple talaq case, the Shabarimala case itself, and ongoing Places of Worship Act litigation. A verdict either way will not just settle who can enter one Kerala temple; it will set or reset the test every future essential-practice dispute gets measured against.

For CLAT, expect the Essential Religious Practices doctrine tested directly, likely asking which case introduced it (Shirur Mutt, 1954) and what Articles 25 and 26 protect respectively. A passage might also test the difference between a review petition and a reference to a larger bench, a procedural distinction the Sabarimala saga illustrates unusually clearly.

topics.title: Kalpakkam's breeder reactor goes critical, and India enters stage two of a 1954 plan
topics.hook: The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam attained first criticality at 8:25 pm on 6 April 2026, making India only the second country after Russia to operate a fast breeder reactor at this scale, and opening the door to the thorium-fuelled third stage of a nuclear programme first sketched by Homi Bhabha in 1954.
topics.story:
\"First criticality\" means a reactor's core has started sustaining a controlled nuclear chain reaction on its own for the first time, the moment a reactor genuinely comes alive rather than merely being switched on. For Kalpakkam's 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor, that moment arrived at 8:25 pm on 6 April 2026, after decades of construction and delay. The reactor is indigenously designed and built, run by Bhavini (Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam), a public-sector company created specifically to build and operate India's fast breeder reactor fleet.

The reason this matters more than a routine plant commissioning is what it unlocks. India's nuclear power programme was structured in three stages by physicist Homi Bhabha as far back as 1954, precisely because India's uranium reserves are modest but its thorium reserves are enormous, roughly a quarter of the world's known deposits, concentrated in coastal monazite sands along states like Kerala and Odisha. Stage one uses natural uranium in pressurised heavy-water reactors, the workhorse design India has run for decades, to generate power and produce plutonium as a byproduct. Stage two, which Kalpakkam's reactor now formally begins, uses that plutonium in fast breeder reactors, which are distinctive because they generate more fissile fuel than they consume, \"breeding\" new material even as they produce power. Stage three, still years away, would use thorium-232 in reactors that convert it, through neutron capture, into uranium-233, a fuel India could sustain almost entirely from domestic resources.

Calling this reactor a \"breeder\" is not a marketing flourish. A conventional reactor burns fuel down over its operating life; a fast breeder reactor's design lets it convert non-fissile uranium-238, which is otherwise unusable as fuel, into new plutonium faster than it burns through its existing fuel load. That property is what makes stage two the hinge between India's uranium-dependent present and its thorium-dependent long-term ambition, since a working breeder programme is the fastest way to accumulate the plutonium stockpile stage three's thorium blanket eventually needs.

India's path here has been slow by any measure: Bhabha's three-stage plan is 72 years old, and Kalpakkam's reactor missed several earlier target dates before finally reaching criticality in April 2026. That timeline is itself worth remembering, because it illustrates how long nuclear infrastructure genuinely takes to build even under a clear, decades-old national plan, a point worth holding against India's newer and faster-moving programmes in areas like quantum communication and semiconductor packaging that made news the same month.

For CLAT, this is classic static-plus-current fusion: examiners can ask who devised the three-stage plan and when (Bhabha, 1954), what fuel each stage uses, why thorium matters strategically for a country with limited uranium, and what \"criticality\" technically means, all anchored to one dated, verifiable April 2026 event.

topics.title: Three months after Maduro's capture, Chevron signs a deal in Caracas
topics.hook: On 13 April 2026, Chevron signed an agreement with Venezuela's interim government at Miraflores Palace, three months after a US military operation captured President Nicolás Maduro, a chapter in the two-century pattern of American intervention that began with the Monroe Doctrine of 1823.
topics.story:
On 3 January 2026, US President Donald Trump announced a large-scale American strike inside Venezuela and said US forces had captured President Nicolás Maduro, ending his 13-year rule and, before that, the broader 27-year period of chavista government that began under Hugo Chávez in 1999. By April, the country was being administered by interim President Delcy Rodríguez, a Maduro-era vice president who stayed on to manage the transition the US was overseeing from outside. On 13 April, Chevron, the American oil major that had operated in Venezuela even through years of US sanctions on the Maduro government, signed a new agreement with the interim administration at Miraflores Palace, the seat of Venezuelan government in Caracas — a striking image, an American company inking a deal in the same building Maduro had governed from days earlier.

Change on the ground has been slower than the speed of the military operation might suggest. Venezuela's National Assembly passed a limited amnesty law covering political offences committed between 1999 and 2026, under which opposition figure Freddy Superlano was released from house arrest. But the deeper reconstruction of Venezuelan institutions, courts, security services, an economy battered by hyperinflation and years of sanctions, is understood to be a multi-year project, not something a single military operation resolves.

The intervention itself sits inside a much older American doctrine. In 1823, President James Monroe told Congress, in what became known as the Monroe Doctrine, that the Western Hemisphere was closed to further European colonisation and that the United States would treat any European effort to control an American state as a hostile act. Over two centuries the doctrine has been invoked, reinterpreted and stretched, from Theodore Roosevelt's 1904 Corollary asserting a US right to intervene in Latin American states' internal affairs, to Cold War-era interventions against left-leaning governments across the hemisphere. Venezuela's own self-description as the \"Bolivarian Republic,\" named for independence leader Simón Bolívar, and its founding membership of OPEC in 1960, sit awkwardly against a country now under direct American oversight of its political transition.

Venezuela holds the world's largest proven oil reserves, a fact central to why a country of just under 30 million people commands this much great-power attention. It joined OPEC as one of five founding members in 1960, alongside Iran, Iraq, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, precisely to give oil-exporting states collective leverage over pricing that individual countries lacked. The Organization of American States, the hemispheric body Venezuela's government has clashed with for years, now faces its own test of relevance in overseeing or endorsing whatever government eventually replaces the current transitional arrangement.

A CLAT passage here would likely test the Monroe Doctrine's date and content directly, ask you to place this intervention inside the broader pattern of hemispheric US interventions, and probe Venezuela's OPEC membership and oil-reserve status as background static knowledge the passage assumes you already have.

topics.title: Orban's sixteen years end as Hungary elects Peter Magyar
topics.hook: Viktor Orban conceded defeat on 12 April 2026 after Peter Magyar's Tisza Party won 138 of 199 seats in Hungary's parliament, ending sixteen years of Orban's rule and a governing style Brussels had long treated as a European Union outlier.
topics.story:
Viktor Orban first became Prime Minister of Hungary in 1998 for a single term, returned to power in 2010, and governed continuously from then until this April, sixteen unbroken years that made him one of the longest-serving leaders in the EU and, for much of that run, a reference point for the kind of \"illiberal democracy\" he openly described as his governing philosophy. His Fidesz party used its supermajorities to rewrite Hungary's constitution, redraw electoral boundaries in its own favour, and bring courts and much of the media under closer government influence, all while remaining inside the EU and eligible for its funding, a combination that made Hungary a recurring flashpoint in EU rule-of-law debates for over a decade.

Peter Magyar, the man who beat him, was until 2023 an insider in Orban's own political circle before breaking away and founding the centre-right Tisza Party. His campaign centred on corruption inside the Orban government and Hungary's underwhelming economic performance relative to its EU neighbours, carried deliberately into smaller cities and rural areas that had long been considered safely Fidesz territory. Turnout surged to nearly 80 percent, an unusually high figure for Hungary, and Tisza took 138 of 199 seats on 53.6 percent of the vote, a supermajority, against Fidesz's 55 seats on 37.8 percent. Orban conceded the same day results became clear, on 12 April.

The defeat is notable partly for how it happened despite Fidesz's structural advantages: a electoral map widely described as gerrymandered in the party's favour, dominant control of state and allied media, and allegations of deepfake videos and vote-buying deployed against the opposition. None of it was enough against a campaign that made corruption and economic stagnation, rather than culture-war issues, its central argument.

Magyar has promised to steer Hungary back toward closer alignment with the EU's judicial and rule-of-law norms, a reversal of a decade of friction between Budapest and Brussels over issues ranging from judicial independence to LGBT rights legislation to Hungary's comparatively friendly posture toward Russia during the Ukraine war. For the EU, Orban's departure removes the bloc's most consistent internal veto-wielder on issues from Ukraine aid to sanctions policy, since EU decisions in several key areas require unanimity among all 27 member states, a rule Orban used repeatedly to extract concessions or simply block consensus.

For CLAT, this pairs naturally with EU institutional questions: the unanimity requirement in areas like foreign policy and enlargement, and how a single member state's veto has historically stalled EU decisions. It is also a clean comparative-politics case study on democratic backsliding and electoral reversal, worth holding against Hungary's EU accession in 2004 as background static knowledge.

topics.title: Amaravati becomes Andhra Pradesh's sole capital, a decade-old question finally closed
topics.hook: Parliament passed the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026 on 1-2 April, giving Amaravati statutory and retrospective status as Andhra Pradesh's sole and permanent capital, closing a capital-city dispute that has run since the state split from Telangana in 2014.
topics.story:
When the original Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act carved Telangana out as a separate state in 2014, it left residual Andhra Pradesh without a capital, since Hyderabad, the shared capital during a transition period, went to Telangana permanently after a set number of years. What followed was a decade of shifting plans: an initial push to build Amaravati as a grand, purpose-built capital city on the Krishna river, a change of state government that shelved that plan in favour of three separate capitals for administrative, legislative and judicial functions, and eventually a return to power for the coalition that had originally championed Amaravati.

The Lok Sabha passed the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026 on 1 April, and the Rajya Sabha followed on 2 April, giving Amaravati formal statutory recognition as the state's sole and permanent capital. President Droupadi Murmu gave her assent on 7 April, and the law was written to apply retrospectively from 2 June 2024, the date the current state government took office, closing off any future government's ability to reopen the three-capitals question through ordinary legislative means. The YSR Congress Party, which had championed the three-capitals plan when it held power, staged a walkout in protest, but the bill otherwise passed with support from both treasury and opposition benches.

The episode is a useful, current illustration of how India actually handles state reorganisation: under Article 3 of the Constitution, Parliament can form new states, alter boundaries, or rename states by a simple majority law, a power state legislatures can be consulted on but not veto. The original 2014 bifurcation, and now this capital-status amendment to it, both flow from that same constitutional provision, which is one reason Parliament, rather than any court, has been the final word on Andhra Pradesh's capital question throughout.

For CLAT, this is a compact, low-effort-to-remember example of Article 3 in live operation, useful for questions distinguishing which body decides state boundary and capital questions (Parliament, by ordinary law) from which body handles constitutional amendments needing special majorities (as tested elsewhere this same month by the 131st Amendment). It is also a reminder that \"reorganisation\" acts are amendable by further ordinary legislation, exactly as happened here twelve years after the original 2014 Act.

topics.title: RBI holds the repo rate at 5.25% as a war it didn't start reshapes its options
topics.hook: The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee met from 6 to 8 April 2026 and unanimously left the repo rate unchanged at 5.25%, judging that a supply-side shock from the West Asia conflict called for watching rather than reacting.
topics.story:
The Monetary Policy Committee, a six-member body that decides India's key interest rates, held its 60th meeting from 6 to 8 April 2026, the first bi-monthly policy statement of the 2026-27 financial year, chaired by RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra. The outcome was a unanimous vote to hold the repo rate, the rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks and the lever it uses to influence borrowing costs across the economy, at 5.25 percent, alongside a continued \"neutral\" policy stance, meaning the committee is signalling neither a bias toward future cuts nor future hikes.

The reasoning given was specifically about the nature of the shock India faces. The MPC's statement pointed to heightened geopolitical risk from the ongoing West Asia conflict, which had disrupted global supply chains and pushed volatility into energy and commodity prices. A central bank's usual toolkit, raising or cutting rates to manage demand, works best against demand-side inflation, price rises caused by too much spending chasing too few goods. A supply-side shock, prices rising because oil and shipping costs have spiked for reasons unrelated to domestic demand, responds differently, and can even be made worse by an ill-timed rate move. The MPC's judgment was that raising rates would do little to fix an oil-price spike caused by tanker traffic being disrupted in the Strait of Hormuz, while cutting rates risked adding unwanted stimulus at a moment of external uncertainty. A pause, in that logic, was the least-bad option.

The committee scheduled its next meeting for 3 to 5 June 2026, leaving itself room to reassess once more was known about how the ceasefire then in place around the Hormuz situation would hold.

For CLAT, expect the Monetary Policy Committee's basic structure tested: it is a six-member body under the RBI Act (as amended in 2016), with the RBI Governor as chairperson, that meets bi-monthly and decides rates by majority vote (unanimous here, but not always). A passage might also test the demand-side versus supply-side inflation distinction directly, since it is the analytical spine of why the RBI chose to hold rather than move.

topics.title: India slips to sixth-largest economy on the IMF's April table, without actually getting poorer
topics.hook: The IMF's April 2026 World Economic Outlook ranks India sixth by nominal GDP, behind the US, China, Germany, Japan and the UK, a fall from earlier fourth-place projections driven not by weaker growth but by a weaker rupee and a technical statistical revision.
topics.story:
India's GDP growth actually accelerated in the year covered, to 7.6 percent in FY26 from 7.1 percent in FY25, keeping it the fastest-growing major economy in the world by the World Bank's own description in its India Development Update released 9 April 2026. Growth for FY27 is projected to moderate to around 6.6 percent, reflecting headwinds from the ongoing Middle East conflict working their way through energy prices and trade. None of that reads like a story about India losing ground.

Yet the IMF's April 2026 World Economic Outlook placed India sixth in nominal GDP terms, at roughly $4.15 trillion, a step down from projections earlier in the cycle that had put India as high as fourth. Two purely technical factors explain the gap between real economic performance and the ranking. First, the rupee depreciated meaningfully against the dollar over the period, from about 84.6 to 88.5 per dollar; since nominal GDP comparisons across countries convert local currency to a common dollar figure, a weaker rupee mechanically shrinks India's dollar-measured GDP even if rupee-measured output is growing fine. Second, India's Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation revised the GDP base year in February 2026, shifting it from 2011-12 to 2022-23, a routine statistical updating exercise that nonetheless lowered the nominal GDP estimate by roughly 4 percent through changed weighting and methodology.

Other indicators in the same reports read more straightforwardly positive. India's current account deficit stood at about 1 percent of GDP, a comfortable level by historical standards, and the general government fiscal deficit continued its gradual consolidation toward 7.4 percent of GDP (a combined centre-plus-states figure, wider than the centre's own fiscal deficit target alone). Employment rates held stable and formal job creation strengthened over the period.

The episode is a useful lesson in reading economic rankings critically: a country's position on a nominal-GDP league table can move for reasons that have nothing to do with whether its economy is actually doing better or worse, which is exactly why economists prefer growth rates and purchasing-power-parity comparisons for judging underlying performance rather than nominal dollar rankings alone.

For CLAT, this is a rare invitation to test genuine economic literacy rather than rote fact recall: can a student explain why a rupee depreciation lowers a dollar-denominated GDP ranking without the underlying economy shrinking, and why statisticians periodically revise GDP base years in the first place.

topics.title: BJP wins a third Assam term as Kerala swings back to Congress
topics.hook: Assam, Kerala and Puducherry voted in a single phase on 9 April 2026, with Assam recording 84.4% turnout as the BJP secured a third straight term on its own strength, while Kerala's Left Democratic Front lost to the Congress-led United Democratic Front.
topics.story:
Assam, Kerala and Puducherry went to the polls together on 9 April 2026, part of the same election cycle that also covered Tamil Nadu and West Bengal later in the month. Assam recorded about 84.4 percent turnout and delivered Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma's BJP a third consecutive term, this time with a majority won on the party's own seats rather than needing its full alliance to cross the line, a stronger mandate than its 2021 win. Kerala moved the other way: voters ended the Left Democratic Front's run, a Communist Party of India (Marxist)-led coalition, in favour of the Congress-led United Democratic Front, continuing Kerala's long-standing pattern of alternating between LDF and UDF governments roughly every five years rather than re-electing an incumbent. Puducherry, the smaller Union Territory contest held the same day, completed the three-way count.

Together with Tamil Nadu and West Bengal, this made 2026 a five-state election cycle unusually consequential for reading India's post-2024 political map: the BJP consolidated in the Northeast while losing ground in the east (West Bengal it actually won) and made no dent in the south beyond a single Tamil Nadu seat, while Congress and its allies recovered specifically in Kerala.

For CLAT, the useful anchor is Kerala's alternation pattern itself, a genuinely unusual feature of Indian state politics worth knowing as a standalone fact, alongside Assam's status as the only Northeast state where the BJP has governed continuously since 2016.

topics.title: India switches on a 1,000 km quantum-secure communication line
topics.hook: India's Department of Science and Technology announced on 8 April 2026 a fully indigenous, 1,000-kilometre secure quantum communication network built by the startup QNu Labs under the National Quantum Mission, a step toward encryption that classical computers, and future quantum ones, cannot break by brute force.
topics.story:
Quantum key distribution uses the physical properties of individual photons to share an encryption key between two points in a way that any attempt to intercept the signal detectably disturbs it, unlike classical encryption, which is secure only because breaking it takes too long with current computers. The concern driving investment here is that sufficiently powerful quantum computers, once built, could break much of today's classical encryption quickly, a risk cryptographers call \"harvest now, decrypt later,\" where adversaries collect encrypted data today to decrypt once quantum computers mature. The 1,000 km network announced on 8 April 2026, built by Bengaluru-founded startup QNu Labs, is India's largest indigenous demonstration of the technology so far.

The project sits under the National Quantum Mission, a government programme approved with an outlay of roughly ₹6,000 crore over 2023-2031 to build capability across quantum computing, communication, sensing and materials, run through the Department of Science and Technology. Placed alongside Kalpakkam's fast breeder reactor milestone the same month, it illustrates two very different paces of Indian technology development: a nuclear programme executing a 72-year-old plan versus a quantum communication startup moving from mission approval to a 1,000 km field demonstration within about three years.

For CLAT, expect the basic principle of quantum key distribution tested (detection of interception via photon disturbance) rather than deep physics, plus the National Quantum Mission's identity as a distinct government mission alongside better-known programmes like the National AI Mission.

topics.title: Parliament decriminalises another batch of minor offences under Jan Vishwas 2.0
topics.hook: Parliament passed the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Bill, 2026 in early April, extending a decriminalisation drive that began in 2023 by converting more minor regulatory offences from criminal penalties into civil fines.
topics.story:
The Jan Vishwas Bill lineage exists to solve a specific problem: Indian law, accumulated over decades, criminalised a large number of minor regulatory lapses, technical paperwork errors, small compliance failures, that carried potential jail time even though nobody involved intended real harm. The original Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 amended 42 central laws to strip out or soften such provisions, replacing possible imprisonment with monetary penalties in many cases, and was pitched explicitly as an ease-of-doing-business and \"trust-based governance\" measure. The 2026 Bill continues that project, amending a further set of enactments to decriminalise or rationalise offences, revising fines to be proportionate to the actual offence rather than fixed at old, often outdated levels.

The underlying philosophy, that the state should reserve criminal law for genuine wrongdoing and handle honest regulatory mistakes through civil penalties instead, has been a recurring theme of the government's legislative programme, running alongside broader criminal-law reform such as the replacement of the colonial-era Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in 2023.

For CLAT, the useful anchor is simply naming the concept correctly, decriminalisation of minor offences as a distinct policy strand from criminal-law codification, and knowing that this is now a repeated legislative exercise (2023, then 2026) rather than a one-off reform.

topics.title: Odisha lays the foundation for India's first 3D glass chip packaging plant
topics.hook: Odisha broke ground on 19 April 2026 for India's first Advanced Glass Semiconductor Packaging Unit in Bhubaneswar, a ₹1,943 crore facility using glass substrates, not silicon, to stack chips for AI and defence electronics.
topics.story:
Semiconductor manufacturing has two broad stages: fabrication, making the actual chip, and packaging, protecting and connecting that chip so it can be soldered into a device. This project belongs to the second stage, and to a specific advanced technique within it: 3D Heterogeneous Integration, which stacks multiple chip components vertically rather than laying them flat, using glass substrates instead of the more common organic or silicon materials because glass offers better electrical and thermal performance for high-density stacking. The Bhubaneswar unit, laid at Info Valley in Khordha district on 19 April 2026, carries a project cost of about ₹1,943 crore, split between roughly ₹799 crore in central government support and about ₹399.5 crore from the Odisha state government, with the remainder from private investment.

The facility is designed to produce 70,000 glass panels and 50 million assembled chip units annually once fully operational, targeted for around 2030, and it makes Odisha the first Indian state to host both a compound semiconductor fabrication unit and an advanced glass-substrate packaging facility, positioning the state as a specific node in India's broader semiconductor push under the India Semiconductor Mission.

For CLAT, the useful distinction is fabrication versus packaging as two separate stages of chip-making, since current-affairs questions on India's semiconductor push often assume you can tell a fab announcement from a packaging announcement.

topics.title: Three April rulings, three different limits on state power
topics.hook: Three separate April 2026 Supreme Court rulings, on dismissing a policeman without inquiry, on whether cooperative milk unions count as 'State,' and on a mandatory step in criminal trials, each narrowed how far an authority can act without giving someone a chance to answer first.
topics.story:
In the first, the Supreme Court set aside the dismissal of a Delhi Police constable, holding that Article 311(2)(b), which lets the government dispense with a departmental inquiry before dismissing an employee in specific extraordinary circumstances, cannot be invoked on mere assumptions without supporting material on record. The provision exists for genuine emergencies where holding a full inquiry is impracticable; the Court's point was that officers cannot treat it as a shortcut whenever an inquiry would simply be inconvenient.

In the second, a bench of Justices B.V. Nagarathna and R. Mahadevan ruled in a Rajasthan dispute that District Milk Unions, cooperative societies managing dairy cooperatives, are independent bodies not amenable to a High Court's writ jurisdiction, because they are not \"instrumentalities of the State\" under Article 12. That article defines \"State\" broadly enough to include bodies substantially controlled or funded by government, and this ruling drew a line excluding cooperative societies that operate with genuine independence despite some regulatory oversight.

In the third, in Shivaji Gangadhar Ingale v. State of Maharashtra, the Court reiterated that putting every incriminating circumstance to the accused under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is mandatory, not a formality courts can skip, since it is the accused's opportunity to personally explain evidence against them before conviction. The same broader roundup also saw the Court reaffirm that FIRs in serious offences like rape cannot ordinarily be quashed merely because the parties reached a private settlement, since such offences carry a grave societal impact beyond the two individuals involved.

For CLAT, treat these as a set: three different provisions (Article 311, Article 12, Section 313 CrPC), one shared theme, that state and quasi-state power comes with mandatory procedural checks courts will not let authorities skip.

topics.title: CSE's State of India's Environment 2026 flags floods, heat and a monitoring gap
topics.hook: The Centre for Science and Environment's annual State of India's Environment report, published in April 2026, warns that flood risk is rising with climate change even as gaps persist in India's air-pollution monitoring network, in a report series that has run since 1982.
topics.story:
The Centre for Science and Environment, a Delhi-based research and advocacy body founded by environmentalist Anil Agarwal, has published State of India's Environment annually since 1982, making it one of the longest-running independent environmental assessments of any country. The 2026 edition centres on floods in a changing climate as its lead theme, alongside chapters on biodiversity, waste and plastics, water and rivers, public health, energy, heat and habitat, and air pollution, plus newer additions this year on artificial intelligence's environmental footprint and demographic change.

The report's core warning is that India's exposure to flooding is intensifying as rainfall patterns become more erratic under climate change, even as monitoring infrastructure for problems like air pollution has not kept pace with the scale of the problem it is meant to track. It sits against a global backdrop the report also references: growing expert concern that the world may soon breach the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C warming threshold, a level the agreement's signatories committed to treating as a critical limit rather than a target to approach.

For CLAT, know CSE as an organisation (founded by Anil Agarwal, publishing since 1982) distinct from government bodies like the Ministry of Environment, since questions sometimes test whether a given report is an official government publication or an independent civil-society one.

topics.title: Two housekeeping bills, a shared paramilitary command and a faster bankruptcy process
topics.hook: Parliament passed the Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Bill and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Bill in early April 2026, tidying up how paramilitary forces are administered and how stressed companies are resolved.
topics.story:
The CAPF (General Administration) Bill, passed by voice vote in early April, brought the administrative and service rules of India's various Central Armed Police Forces, forces like the CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP and SSB, onto a more unified statutory footing, rather than each force operating under its own separately evolved set of rules and precedents. These forces sit under the Union Ministry of Home Affairs and together form the backbone of India's internal security, border-guarding and VIP-protection apparatus, distinct from the Army, Navy and Air Force, which report to the Ministry of Defence and handle external defence.

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Bill, passed by the Rajya Sabha the same period by voice vote, made further procedural changes to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the law that created a time-bound process for resolving companies unable to pay their debts, replacing an older, slower patchwork of recovery mechanisms. Amendments to the IBC have become a near-annual exercise since 2016 as regulators and courts identify procedural gaps the original law did not anticipate.

For CLAT, the useful distinction is institutional: CAPFs report to the Home Ministry and handle internal security, while the armed forces report to Defence and handle external threats, a distinction current-affairs questions test more often than the specific content of either April bill.

topics.title: India's envoy calls on Bangladesh's new PM as ties reset post-Hasina
topics.hook: India's High Commissioner to Bangladesh, Pranay Verma, paid a courtesy call on Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on 6 April 2026, part of a cautious diplomatic reset after the political upheaval that removed Sheikh Hasina from power.
topics.story:
Bangladesh's political order shifted sharply after Sheikh Hasina's government fell amid mass protests, ending her long tenure as Prime Minister and opening a period of transitional governance before elections eventually brought Tarique Rahman, long the exiled acting chairperson of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, into the Prime Minister's office. The change mattered enormously for India, which had built an unusually close working relationship with Hasina's Awami League government over 15 years, and had to recalibrate its approach to a BNP-led administration historically seen as warier of New Delhi and more open to China and Pakistan.

The 6 April courtesy call between High Commissioner Pranay Verma and PM Tarique Rahman was a modest, largely symbolic diplomatic step, both sides describing it as focused on \"people-centric\" cooperation, but it signalled that formal channels between the two governments were functioning normally despite the change of regime. The broader relationship carries real stakes for India: Bangladesh borders four Indian states, shares the Ganga and Teesta river systems whose water-sharing has long been contentious, and sits along transit routes India uses to connect its Northeastern states to the rest of the country.

For CLAT, the useful anchor is simply naming the current Bangladeshi leadership correctly and knowing why India-Bangladesh relations carry outsized strategic weight relative to the size of the bilateral relationship, given the border, river-sharing, and Northeast-connectivity dimensions.

topics.title: Myanmar's junta chief wins an indirect presidential vote he engineered
topics.hook: Myanmar held an indirect presidential election on 3 April 2026, five years after the 2021 military coup, and Min Aung Hlaing, the general who led that coup, won the presidency through a process his own military-appointed electoral college controlled.
topics.story:
Myanmar's military, the Tatmadaw, seized power in February 2021, overthrowing Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government and detaining her along with much of her party's leadership, plunging the country into a civil conflict between the junta and a patchwork of resistance forces that has continued for five years. The 3 April 2026 presidential election was indirect, decided not by popular vote but by an electoral college structured under rules the military itself set, and Min Aung Hlaing, who had led the coup and subsequently headed the ruling council, won the presidency, with Nyo Saw and Nan Ni Ni Aye elected vice presidents.

The vote's significance lies less in genuine electoral competition, which most independent observers say did not meaningfully exist, than in what it signals: an attempt by the junta to convert five years of military rule into a nominally civilian, constitutionally dressed presidency, a familiar playbook in countries where militaries seek durable political control without formally abandoning electoral institutions.

For CLAT, know the basic sequence, 2021 coup, ongoing civil conflict, 2026 indirect presidential vote, and be able to identify Min Aung Hlaing by name and role, a standard current-affairs check on Southeast Asian political developments.

topics.title: Asha Bhosle, voice of seven decades of Hindi cinema, dies at 92
topics.hook: Playback singer Asha Bhosle died on 12 April 2026 in Mumbai at 92, after recording an estimated 12,000 songs across multiple Indian languages over a career spanning roughly seven decades.
topics.story:
Asha Bhosle began recording as a child performer in the 1940s and built, over the following decades, one of the largest and most versatile bodies of work in Indian film music, ranging across classical-influenced compositions, cabaret numbers, and later collaborations that took her sound into electronic and Western-fusion territory well into her seventies and eighties. She died at Breach Candy Hospital in Mumbai on 12 April 2026, where she had been admitted for exhaustion and a chest infection, at the age of 92.

Both Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Droupadi Murmu issued statements marking her death, Murmu describing it as \"an irreparable loss to music lovers.\" Bhosle's career sat alongside, and for decades in the shadow of, her elder sister Lata Mangeshkar, who died in 2022; between them the two sisters are commonly credited with providing the singing voice for the overwhelming majority of Hindi film heroines across nearly the entire history of playback singing in Indian cinema.

For CLAT, this belongs to the obituary category current-affairs papers test lightly but reliably: know the name, the rough career span, and her place alongside Lata Mangeshkar as the two defining voices of Hindi playback singing.

topics.story:

topics.title: PM Mudra Yojana turns 11, still India's biggest small-loan scheme
topics.hook: The Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana marked 11 years since its April 2015 launch, continuing to provide collateral-free loans of up to ₹20 lakh to small and micro entrepreneurs who fall outside conventional bank lending.
topics.story:
Launched on 8 April 2015, Mudra Yojana addresses a specific gap: very small businesses, street vendors, small manufacturers, tiny service providers, that are too small and undocumented for conventional bank loans, which typically require collateral and financial history these borrowers cannot supply. Loans under the scheme are categorised into three tiers by size: Shishu (up to ₹50,000), Kishor (₹50,000 to ₹5 lakh), and Tarun (₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh), with a fourth Tarun Plus tier added later extending the ceiling to ₹20 lakh for borrowers who had successfully repaid earlier Tarun loans.

The scheme is implemented through the Micro Units Development and Refinance Agency (MUDRA), a non-banking financial institution set up specifically to refinance the banks, non-banking financial companies, and microfinance institutions that make these loans to end borrowers, rather than lending to individuals directly itself.

For CLAT, know the loan-tier names and ceilings (Shishu, Kishor, Tarun, Tarun Plus) as the most exam-friendly detail, since scheme-anniversary questions often test specific numbers over general description.

topics.title: Ladakh keeps pushing for Sixth Schedule status, and Delhi keeps promising talks
topics.hook: Activist Sonam Wangchuk, released in March after six months in detention, told reporters on 7 April 2026 that Ladakh's demands for statehood and Sixth Schedule protections needed 'open-minded and sincere' talks, ahead of Union Home Minister Amit Shah's scheduled 30 April visit.
topics.story:
Ladakh has been governed as a Union Territory without a legislature since 2019, when it was carved out of the former state of Jammu and Kashmir, and its residents have pressed since then for two connected demands: full statehood, or at least a legislature, and inclusion under the Constitution's Sixth Schedule, which grants tribal areas in the Northeast a measure of local self-governance over land, forests and customary law through Autonomous District Councils. Sonam Wangchuk, an engineer and education reformer turned Ladakh rights activist, has become the most visible face of that campaign, including through prolonged hunger strikes, and was detained under the National Security Act for six months before his release on 14 March 2026.

On 7 April, days after his release, Wangchuk pressed the government for genuine dialogue rather than a symbolic process, and on 26 April the Leh Apex Body, one of the two main civil-society coalitions leading the movement, held its own meeting and press conference restating its demands. Union Home Minister Amit Shah was scheduled to visit Ladakh on 30 April, ahead of formal Centre-Ladakh talks planned for 22 May 2026.

For CLAT, know the Sixth Schedule's actual content, Autonomous District Councils for Northeast tribal areas under Articles 244(2) and 275(1), since Ladakh's demand to be brought under a Northeast-specific constitutional provision, despite being nowhere near the Northeast, is itself the kind of detail an exam likes to probe.

passages.title: The bill that won more votes than it lost, and still failed
passages.passage:
On 17 April 2026, the Lok Sabha voted on the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026. Of 528 members present, 298 voted in favour and 230 against. By the standard of an ordinary law, this was a comfortable win. The bill still failed, because Article 368 of the Constitution requires that certain amendments, including this one, secure not a simple majority but a majority of the total membership of the House plus two-thirds of the members present and voting. Two-thirds of 528 is 352. The bill fell 54 votes short.

The stakes were real. The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 had already reserved one-third of Lok Sabha and state assembly seats for women, but tied that reservation's activation to delimitation carried out after \"the first census taken after 2026,\" a phrase written into the Constitution by earlier amendments that froze Lok Sabha seat numbers at 1971 levels. Waiting for a full post-census delimitation cycle threatened to push the women's quota into the 2030s. The 131st Amendment tried to shortcut that wait by using 2011 Census data instead and simultaneously expanding the Lok Sabha from 543 to 850 seats.

That expansion is exactly what sank the bill. States that had slowed their population growth through decades of development, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Odisha among them, stood to lose relative seat share under a population-based formula, since faster-growing northern states would gain proportionally more seats. Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M.K. Stalin called the bill a \"historic injustice\" and led black-flag protests the day it was introduced. When the amendment failed, two dependent bills, the Delimitation Bill, 2026 and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, were withdrawn the same day, since neither could function without the constitutional change collapsing under them.

The 106th Amendment remains law. It is simply still waiting for a delimitation exercise Parliament could not agree how, or how fast, to conduct.

questions.q: What was the primary reason the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 failed despite winning more votes than it lost?
options: The President refused to grant assent
It did not secure the two-thirds majority of members present and voting required under Article 368
The Rajya Sabha rejected it after Lok Sabha passage
It was struck down by the Supreme Court before the vote
questions.explain: The passage states the bill needed 352 votes (two-thirds of 528 present) under Article 368 but received only 298. It never reached the Rajya Sabha or a court; the vote itself decided the outcome.

questions.q: Which constitutional amendment had already reserved one-third of Lok Sabha and state assembly seats for women before the 131st Amendment was introduced?
options: The 84th Amendment
The 87th Amendment
The 106th Amendment
The 131st Amendment itself
questions.explain: The 106th Amendment (2023) is described as having already reserved the seats, with its activation tied to delimitation. The 131st Amendment tried, and failed, to make that reservation usable sooner.

questions.q: Based on the passage, why did states like Tamil Nadu and Kerala oppose the bill?
options: They opposed women's reservation in principle
They wanted the census delayed further
A population-based seat expansion threatened to reduce their relative political representation because their population growth had slowed
They demanded a different capital city arrangement
questions.explain: The passage explicitly links southern-state opposition to seat-share loss under population-based expansion, not to opposition to women's reservation itself, which the bill was meant to help implement.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true according to the passage?
options: The Delimitation Bill, 2026 passed even after the 131st Amendment failed
The 106th Amendment Act, 2023 was invalidated when the 131st Amendment failed
Two dependent bills were withdrawn the same day the 131st Amendment failed
The vote count was 352 in favour and 298 against
questions.explain: The passage states the Delimitation Bill and UT Laws Amendment Bill were withdrawn the same day. The 106th Amendment 'remains law,' and the actual vote was 298 for, 230 against, not the figures in the other options.

questions.q: The passage mentions Lok Sabha seats being frozen at '1971 levels.' Which constitutional amendment originally imposed this freeze?
options: The 42nd Amendment (1976)
The 44th Amendment (1978)
The 73rd Amendment (1992)
The 91st Amendment (2003)
questions.explain: This detail is outside the passage itself and draws on static constitutional knowledge: the 42nd Amendment of 1976 first froze Lok Sabha seat numbers at 1971 Census levels, later extended by the 84th and 87th Amendments.

passages.title: One dynasty breaks, another falls: two state elections, two different endings
passages.passage:
India's April 2026 state election cycle produced two results that, on the surface, look similar, incumbents losing ground, but that actually tell opposite stories about how power changes hands.

In Tamil Nadu, no party or alliance won a majority for the first time since the DMK first took power in 1967. Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam, the party actor Vijay launched in 2024, became the single largest party with 108 of 234 seats, ten short of the 118 needed to govern alone. The DMK-led alliance fell to 73 seats, and the AIADMK-led alliance to 53, with the BJP managing just a single seat despite contesting in alliance. Tamil Nadu now has its first hung assembly in nearly six decades, an outcome that hands TVK outsized influence without handing it outright power.

West Bengal's story ran differently. The BJP won 206 of 293 contested seats, enough to govern on its own, ending Mamata Banerjee's Trinamool Congress government after fifteen unbroken years. Banerjee herself won her own seat, Bhabanipur, even as her party lost its majority statewide, a split result that shows a leader's personal popularity surviving even when her party's broader mandate does not. Voting in West Bengal ran across two phases, on 23 and 29 April, a scheduling choice the Election Commission uses in large or security-sensitive states to manage the deployment of polling personnel and security forces.

Both results share a root cause worth noticing: voters in both states rejected an incumbent, but the shape of that rejection, a genuinely new third force in Tamil Nadu, a clean alternation of power in Bengal, differed enough that treating them as the same story would miss what each actually reveals about how India's regional party systems are evolving.

options: Both states elected the BJP to power
Both results look similar on the surface but reflect different underlying political dynamics
Both states had their elections postponed
Both incumbents were re-elected with increased majorities
questions.explain: The passage's opening and closing frame this explicitly: superficially similar (incumbents losing ground), but substantively different (a hung assembly with a new party versus a clean alternation of power).

options: 5 seats
10 seats
12 seats
20 seats
questions.explain: The passage states TVK won 108 of 234 seats, 'ten short of the 118 needed to govern alone.'

questions.q: What can be inferred about Mamata Banerjee's personal standing from the passage?
options: She lost her own seat along with her party's majority
She retained her own seat even as her party lost its statewide majority
She did not contest the 2026 election
She switched parties before the election
questions.explain: The passage notes she 'won her own seat, Bhabanipur, even as her party lost its majority statewide,' explicitly separating her personal result from her party's.

questions.q: According to the passage, why does the Election Commission sometimes hold elections in phases, as it did in West Bengal?
options: To allow parties more time to campaign
To manage deployment of polling personnel and security forces in large or security-sensitive states
Because the Constitution mandates phased voting for all states
To accommodate different regional languages
questions.explain: The passage directly states this reason. Phased polling is an administrative and security tool, not a constitutional requirement or a campaign-related accommodation.
