options: M.G. Ramachandran split from the DMK in 1972 to found the AIADMK
The AIADMK was founded before the DMK
The AIADMK is a breakaway faction of the Indian National Congress
The AIADMK was founded by C.N. Annadurai
questions.explain: This draws on static knowledge beyond the passage: M.G. Ramachandran (MGR) split from the DMK in 1972 and founded the AIADMK, which won power in 1977. Annadurai founded the DMK, not the AIADMK.

passages.title: Why two countries that don't border the Gulf convened a summit about it
passages.passage:
On 17 April 2026, France and the United Kingdom convened 51 countries in an International Summit on the Strait of Hormuz. Neither co-chair, President Emmanuel Macron nor Prime Minister Keir Starmer, governs a Gulf state. Both, however, sit on the UN Security Council as permanent members, and both have long treated freedom-of-navigation disputes as questions for the international system as a whole rather than for regional actors alone.

The war behind the summit began on 28 February 2026, when the United States and Israel struck Iran and killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran retaliated against Israel, American bases across the Gulf, and US-allied Gulf states, and its Revolutionary Guard Corps moved to restrict passage through the Strait of Hormuz itself, boarding ships and laying mines. A ceasefire held for roughly sixty days from early April before collapsing in mid-June, and fighting resumed again in July after Iran struck commercial vessels that had bypassed its approved shipping route.

The geography explains the stakes. The strait separates Iran from Oman across a channel just 33 kilometres wide at its narrowest point, with shipping lanes on either side only 3 kilometres across. Roughly a fifth of the world's traded oil passes through it, alongside a large share of global liquefied natural gas exports. When Iran struck the United Arab Emirates directly in early April, Emirati air defences intercepted 19 ballistic missiles and 26 drones in a single wave, evidence of how far the conflict had spread beyond its original combatants.

India felt the disruption directly: an Indian-flagged tanker, the Jag Vasant, sat stranded in the strait for 23 days before finally docking in Mumbai with an LPG cargo the government had been tracking against fears of a domestic cooking-gas shortage. New Delhi's official response was to express \"deep concern\" and urge restraint on all sides, a studiedly neutral posture that reflects India's competing ties: growing defence and energy partnerships with Israel and the Gulf Arab states, alongside a decades-old relationship with Iran built partly around Chabahar port.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To argue that France and the UK should not have convened the Hormuz summit
To explain the causes, scale and consequences of the Strait of Hormuz crisis, including India's specific stake in it
To provide a technical description of missile defence systems
To compare Iran's military capacity with Israel's
questions.explain: The passage moves from the summit, to the war's origins, to the strait's economic significance, to India's specific exposure, weaving them into a single explanatory account rather than making an argument or a technical or comparative case.

questions.q: Why does the passage note that neither Macron nor Starmer governs a Gulf state?
options: To suggest the summit lacked legitimacy
To highlight that their authority to convene it came from their countries' UN Security Council permanent-member status, not regional proximity
To argue that only Gulf states should decide Hormuz's future
It is an incidental detail with no bearing on the passage's argument
questions.explain: The passage explicitly links their role to permanent UNSC membership and a historical pattern of treating freedom-of-navigation as an international rather than purely regional matter.

questions.q: Which of the following can be inferred about India's official position on the 2026 Iran war?
options: India sided openly with Iran against the US and Israel
India suspended all trade with Gulf states in protest
India adopted a deliberately neutral stance reflecting its competing strategic relationships in the region
India formally joined the 51-nation Hormuz summit as a co-chair
questions.explain: The passage describes India's 'deep concern' and calls for restraint 'on all sides' as reflecting a balance between its Israel/Gulf partnerships and its Iran relationship, not alignment with any single side, and does not mention India as a co-chair.

questions.q: According to the passage, approximately what share of the world's traded oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz?
options: One-tenth
One-fifth
One-third
One-half
questions.explain: The passage states 'roughly a fifth of the world's traded oil passes through it.'

questions.q: The passage refers to India's Chabahar port investment. What is Chabahar port's strategic purpose for India?
options: It is India's largest domestic container port
It gives India an alternate trade route into Afghanistan and Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan
It serves as an Indian naval base in the Persian Gulf
It is the primary loading point for India's oil imports from Saudi Arabia
questions.explain: This draws on background static knowledge the passage assumes: Chabahar, an Iranian port developed with Indian investment, is valued specifically because it lets India reach Afghanistan and Central Asia without transiting Pakistani territory.

passages.title: Ninety-five years without a number
passages.passage:
India began houselisting operations for its 16th decennial census on 1 April 2026, deploying over 34 lakh personnel to count an estimated 1.4 billion people at a budgeted cost of roughly ₹11,718 crore. Two features distinguish this census from every one before it. It is India's first fully digital census, conducted through a mobile application with real-time data upload, and it includes a self-enumeration window, from 1 to 15 April, through which citizens can submit their own household details online rather than waiting for a government enumerator to visit.

The more consequential change is what the census asks. For the first time since 1931, it will collect caste data at the individual level, when the second phase, the Population Enumeration, begins in February 2027. Every British-era census recorded caste; independent India's very first census, in 1951, dropped the question, on the reasoning that counting caste risked entrenching the social hierarchy the Constitution was trying to dismantle. Every reservation-policy debate since, including the 1980 Mandal Commission's recommendations on OBC quotas, has consequently run on survey estimates and extrapolations from that 1931 data rather than an actual updated count, because no comprehensive caste census has existed for nearly a century.

Supporters of the caste question argue that reservation policy deserves to rest on real numbers rather than nine-decade-old extrapolations. Critics, including some minority-community advocacy groups, worry that formalising caste categories built around a historically Hindu framework could complicate matters for Muslim and Christian communities that do not map neatly onto it, and might even entangle questions of documentation or citizenship that have nothing to do with reservation policy at all.

The census itself runs in two phases: houselisting from April to September 2026, and population enumeration from February 2027, meaning the caste data at the centre of the current debate will not actually exist for policymakers to use for close to another year.

questions.q: What is the central concern the passage raises about India's 2026 census?
options: Whether the census will be completed on schedule
Whether the reintroduction of caste data collection, absent since 1931, will help or complicate India's reservation-policy and minority-community debates
Whether the digital census app will function correctly
Whether enough personnel have been deployed
questions.explain: The passage's central tension, laid out across two full paragraphs, is the caste-data question and its contested consequences, not logistics, technology, or staffing, which are mentioned only briefly.

questions.q: According to the passage, what reasoning did independent India's government use to drop the caste question in 1951?
options: Caste data was too expensive to collect
Counting caste risked entrenching the social hierarchy the Constitution sought to dismantle
The British had already collected enough caste data to last a century
State governments objected to a central caste count
questions.explain: The passage states this reasoning explicitly: officials feared entrenching hierarchy rather than dismantling it.

questions.q: Based on the passage, what has India's reservation-policy debate, including the Mandal Commission, relied on in the absence of updated caste data?
options: Real-time state government reports
Survey estimates and extrapolations from the 1931 Census
United Nations demographic models
Data collected informally by political parties
questions.explain: The passage directly states that policy debates 'have consequently run on survey estimates and extrapolations from that 1931 data.'

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the 2026 census is true according to the passage?
options: Caste data will be available by September 2026
The census includes a self-enumeration window from 1 to 15 April 2026
This is India's first digital census as well as its first census overall
The Mandal Commission recommended dropping the caste question
questions.explain: The self-enumeration window is stated explicitly. Caste data comes only in the 2027 phase, this is not India's first census overall (it is the 16th), and the Mandal Commission used, rather than opposed, caste-based data.

questions.q: The passage mentions the 1980 Mandal Commission. What reservation quota did that commission recommend for Other Backward Classes?
options: 15 percent
27 percent
33 percent
50 percent
questions.explain: This is background static knowledge: the Mandal Commission recommended 27 percent reservation for OBCs, based on 1931 caste-census extrapolations, a recommendation the government implemented in 1990.

passages.title: What one Kerala temple case decides for every faith in India
passages.passage:
In September 2018, a five-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court ruled 4-1 that Sabarimala temple's practice of barring women aged roughly ten to fifty from entry violated Articles 14, 15 and 25 of the Constitution. Rather than resolving the flood of review petitions that followed on their individual merits, the Court in 2020 referred a broader set of questions to a larger bench, reasoning that Sabarimala could not be decided in isolation from structurally similar disputes: the entry of Muslim women into mosques, the entry of Parsi women who marry outside the faith into fire temples, and the practice of female genital cutting among the Dawoodi Bohra community. Sixty-six separate matters are now tagged to what is formally called the Sabarimala Reference.

A nine-judge bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant opened hearings on 7 April 2026. Review petitioners argued from 7 to 9 April, the original writ petitioners opposing any reopening of the 2018 verdict argued from 14 to 16 April, and rejoinder and amicus curiae submissions followed on 21 and 22 April. The bench reserved judgment on 14 May, after sixteen days of hearings.

What is genuinely at stake is not Sabarimala alone but the Essential Religious Practices doctrine, the test Indian courts have applied since the 1954 Shirur Mutt case to decide which customs Article 25's freedom-of-religion guarantee actually protects. Under that doctrine, a court must first decide whether a practice is essential to a religion's core theology before it can determine whether the state may regulate it, a role that has long drawn criticism for turning judges into arbiters of theology rather than law. The bench is also weighing Article 26, which protects a religious denomination's right to manage its own affairs, against the equality guarantees of Articles 14 and 15, and considering whether Sabarimala's Ayyappa devotees constitute a distinct religious denomination with rights separate from Hinduism more broadly.

However the bench eventually rules, its answer will not just settle who can enter one Kerala temple. It will set, or reset, the test every future essential-practice dispute in India gets measured against.

questions.q: What is the main idea the passage develops about the Sabarimala Reference?
options: That the case is a narrow dispute limited to one Kerala temple
That the case's real significance lies in reshaping the broader Essential Religious Practices doctrine, affecting many unrelated faith disputes
That the Supreme Court has already ruled in favour of the review petitioners
That the case concerns only procedural questions with no constitutional significance
questions.explain: The passage's final paragraph makes this point explicitly: the ruling 'will not just settle who can enter one Kerala temple,' but reset the doctrine used across all future essential-practice disputes.

questions.q: According to the passage, why did the Supreme Court refer the Sabarimala review petitions to a larger bench in 2020 instead of deciding them directly?
options: The original five judges had all retired
The Court considered the case impossible to decide separately from structurally similar faith-practice disputes elsewhere
The Kerala government requested the referral
The review petitioners withdrew their petitions
questions.explain: The passage states the Court's reasoning directly: it saw Sabarimala as inseparable from similar disputes like mosque entry for Muslim women and fire-temple entry for Parsi women.

questions.q: What does the Essential Religious Practices doctrine require a court to determine, according to the passage?
options: Whether a majority of a religion's followers support a given practice
Whether a practice is essential to a religion's core theology before deciding if the state can regulate it
Whether a practice has existed for at least a century
Whether a practice violates any specific criminal law
questions.explain: The passage defines the doctrine precisely: courts must decide whether a practice is 'essential to a religion's core theology' as a threshold question before assessing whether the state may regulate it.

questions.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage's account of the hearing schedule?
options: The bench decided the case within a single day of hearings
Review petitioners argued after the opposing writ petitioners
Rejoinder and amicus curiae submissions were the final stage before judgment was reserved
The bench reserved judgment before hearing any arguments
questions.explain: The passage sequences the hearings clearly: review petitioners first (7-9 April), opposing petitioners next (14-16 April), then rejoinders and amicus submissions (21-22 April), after which judgment was reserved on 14 May.

questions.q: The passage notes the Essential Religious Practices doctrine originated in the 1954 Shirur Mutt case. What was that case fundamentally about?
options: The extent of state control over the management of a Hindu religious institution
Reservation quotas in government employment
The validity of a state's land reform legislation
Freedom of the press under Article 19
questions.explain: This is background static knowledge: the Shirur Mutt case concerned the extent to which the state could regulate the management of a Hindu Mutt (religious institution), and it was in this context that the Essential Religious Practices test was first articulated.

passages.title: Seventy-two years to stage two
passages.passage:
At 8:25 pm on 6 April 2026, the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam attained first criticality, the moment its core began sustaining a controlled nuclear chain reaction on its own for the first time. The 500 MWe reactor, indigenously designed and built, is operated by Bhavini, a public-sector company created specifically to run India's fast breeder reactor fleet.

The milestone matters because of what it formally begins: stage two of a three-stage nuclear power plan physicist Homi Bhabha devised in 1954, built around a straightforward resource constraint. India's uranium reserves are modest, but its thorium reserves are enormous, roughly a quarter of the world's known deposits, concentrated in coastal monazite sands. Stage one uses natural uranium in pressurised heavy-water reactors to generate power while producing plutonium as a byproduct. Stage two, which Kalpakkam's reactor now advances, uses that plutonium as fuel in fast breeder reactors, so called because they generate more fissile material than they consume, converting non-fissile uranium-238 into new plutonium faster than they burn through their existing fuel. Stage three, still years away, would use thorium-232, converting it through neutron capture into uranium-233, a fuel India could sustain almost entirely from domestic resources.

The achievement puts India in a select group: it becomes only the second country after Russia to operate a fast breeder reactor at this commercial scale. It has also been a slow road. Bhabha's plan is 72 years old, and Kalpakkam's reactor missed several earlier target dates before finally reaching criticality this April, a reminder of how long nuclear infrastructure takes to build even under a clear, long-standing national roadmap.

For India, the strategic logic is specific rather than abstract: a working breeder programme is the fastest way to accumulate the plutonium stockpile that stage three's thorium-fuelled reactors will eventually need, making stage two less a destination than a necessary bridge to stage three's larger ambition.

questions.q: What is the main point the passage makes about the Kalpakkam reactor's significance?
options: It is India's first nuclear power plant of any kind
It formally begins stage two of a long-standing three-stage nuclear plan built around India's thorium reserves
It replaces the need for any further nuclear reactors in India
It was completed exactly on its original 1954 target schedule
questions.explain: The passage frames the reactor's significance specifically as advancing 'stage two' of Bhabha's plan, and explicitly notes the project 'missed several earlier target dates,' contradicting the idea it met an original schedule.

questions.q: Why, according to the passage, does India's nuclear programme rely on a fast breeder reactor as a bridge between stages one and three?
options: Because fast breeder reactors are cheaper to build than any other reactor type
Because a working breeder programme is the fastest way to accumulate the plutonium stockpile stage three's thorium reactors will need
Because fast breeder reactors do not require any uranium at all
Because international law requires countries to operate a breeder reactor before using thorium
questions.explain: The passage's closing paragraph states this directly: the breeder programme accumulates the plutonium stockpile that stage three's thorium-fuelled reactors will eventually require.

questions.q: What does the term 'fast breeder reactor' specifically describe, according to the passage?
options: A reactor that operates only briefly before shutting down
A reactor that generates more fissile material than it consumes by converting uranium-238 into new plutonium
A reactor that uses only thorium as fuel
A reactor built faster than conventional nuclear plants
questions.explain: The passage defines the term precisely: such reactors are 'so called because they generate more fissile material than they consume,' converting uranium-238 into new plutonium.

questions.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: India's uranium reserves exceed its thorium reserves
India holds roughly a quarter of the world's known thorium reserves
The Kalpakkam reactor is operated directly by the Department of Atomic Energy rather than a separate company
India is the first country in the world to operate a fast breeder reactor at commercial scale
questions.explain: The passage states India holds 'roughly a quarter of the world's known deposits' of thorium, against modest uranium reserves. The reactor is operated by Bhavini, a separate public-sector company, and India is the second country after Russia to reach this scale.

questions.q: The passage credits Homi Bhabha with devising India's three-stage nuclear plan in 1954. Which institution did Bhabha also found, closely associated with India's early nuclear and physics research?
options: Indian Institute of Science
Tata Institute of Fundamental Research
Indian Space Research Organisation
Council of Scientific and Industrial Research
questions.explain: This draws on background static knowledge: Homi Bhabha founded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in 1945, which became a cornerstone of India's early nuclear physics research, distinct from ISRO or CSIR.

passages.title: Growing faster, ranking lower: India's April economic snapshot
passages.passage:
Two numbers about the Indian economy circulated in April 2026 that seemed to point in opposite directions. India's GDP growth accelerated to 7.6 percent in FY26, up from 7.1 percent in FY25, keeping it the fastest-growing major economy in the world, according to the World Bank's India Development Update, released 9 April. At the same time, the IMF's April 2026 World Economic Outlook ranked India sixth by nominal GDP, at roughly $4.15 trillion, a step down from earlier projections that had placed it as high as fourth.

The explanation is technical rather than economic. Two factors, unrelated to India's actual output, account for the gap. First, the rupee depreciated over the period, from about 84.6 to 88.5 per US dollar. Because nominal GDP comparisons convert local-currency output into a common dollar figure, a weaker rupee mechanically shrinks India's dollar-measured GDP even while rupee-measured output keeps growing. Second, India's statistics ministry revised the GDP base year in February 2026, from 2011-12 to 2022-23, a routine methodological update that nonetheless lowered the nominal estimate by roughly 4 percent through changed weighting.

Meanwhile, the Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee met from 6 to 8 April and voted unanimously to hold the repo rate at 5.25 percent, citing heightened geopolitical risk from the ongoing West Asia conflict, which had disrupted supply chains and pushed volatility into energy prices. The committee's reasoning turned on a basic distinction: conventional rate moves work best against demand-side inflation, price rises caused by excess spending, but do little to fix a supply-side shock like a war-driven oil-price spike, and can even worsen it if timed badly. A pause, the committee judged, was the least-bad option while it waited to see how the conflict, and any ceasefire, developed.

questions.q: What is the passage's main point about India's GDP growth and its IMF ranking?
options: Both moved in the same direction, confirming India's economic decline
India's actual growth accelerated even as its nominal-dollar GDP ranking fell, for reasons unrelated to real economic performance
The IMF ranking is more reliable than the World Bank's growth figures
India's GDP growth slowed due to the rupee's depreciation
questions.explain: The passage's opening frames this as two numbers 'pointing in opposite directions,' and goes on to explain that the ranking fell due to currency and statistical factors, not slower growth, which in fact accelerated.

questions.q: According to the passage, why does a weaker rupee lower India's ranking on a nominal-dollar GDP table even without any change in real economic output?
options: Because a weaker rupee automatically reduces India's tax revenue
Because nominal GDP comparisons convert local-currency output into dollars, so currency depreciation mechanically shrinks the dollar-converted figure
Because the IMF penalises countries with weaker currencies in its rankings
Because a weaker rupee causes real GDP growth to slow
questions.explain: The passage explains this mechanism directly: dollar-converted comparisons are sensitive to exchange rates, so a weaker rupee shrinks the dollar figure independent of actual output growth.

questions.q: Why, according to the passage, did the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee choose to hold the repo rate rather than change it?
options: Inflation had fallen to zero
The shock facing India was supply-side, driven by the West Asia conflict, which conventional rate moves address poorly
The government instructed the RBI to hold rates
Demand in the economy had collapsed
questions.explain: The passage explains the MPC's reasoning explicitly: a supply-side shock from war-related disruption responds differently to conventional demand-management tools than the RBI usually applies.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true according to the passage?
options: The GDP base year was revised from 2022-23 to 2011-12
India's FY26 growth rate was lower than its FY25 growth rate
The MPC's April 2026 decision to hold the repo rate was unanimous
The IMF ranked India fourth in its April 2026 World Economic Outlook
questions.explain: The passage states the MPC vote was unanimous. The base year revision ran the opposite direction (2011-12 to 2022-23), FY26 growth (7.6%) exceeded FY25 (7.1%), and the IMF ranked India sixth, not fourth.

questions.q: The passage distinguishes demand-side from supply-side inflation. Which of these would most likely be classified as demand-side inflation?
options: Prices rising because a war disrupted oil shipping routes
Prices rising because a poor monsoon damaged crop supply
Prices rising because consumer spending surged after wage increases, without any change in supply
Prices rising because a factory fire cut production of a key input
questions.explain: Demand-side inflation is driven by excess spending relative to supply, as in the wage-driven consumer spending surge; the other three options describe supply disruptions, which the passage identifies as the kind of shock conventional rate policy addresses poorly.

passages.title: Two governments changed hands in April, by very different routes
passages.passage:
Two long-serving governments effectively ended in the weeks around April 2026, though almost nothing else about how they ended was similar.

In Hungary, Viktor Orban conceded defeat on 12 April after sixteen unbroken years in power, during which his Fidesz party used its parliamentary supermajorities to rewrite the constitution, redraw electoral boundaries in its own favour, and bring courts and much of the national media under closer government influence, all while remaining inside the European Union. Peter Magyar, a former Orban-circle insider who broke away in 2023 to found the Tisza Party, led that party to 138 of 199 seats on 53.6 percent of the vote, a supermajority, against Fidesz's 55 seats on 37.8 percent, with turnout surging to nearly 80 percent. Magyar's campaign centred on corruption and economic underperformance, and he has promised to reintegrate Hungary into the EU's judicial norms after a decade of friction over rule-of-law concerns.

Venezuela's transition looked nothing like an election. On 3 January 2026, the United States announced a military strike inside the country and the capture of President Nicolás Maduro, ending 27 years of chavista government that began under Hugo Chávez in 1999. By April, interim President Delcy Rodríguez, a former Maduro-era vice president, was overseeing a US-backed transition, and on 13 April, Chevron signed a new agreement with the interim government at Miraflores Palace, the same building Maduro had governed from months earlier. A limited amnesty law freed some political prisoners, but observers cautioned that rebuilding Venezuela's courts, security services and sanctions-battered economy would take years, not months.

One government fell to a ballot box after a fair, if hard-fought, contest. The other fell to foreign military force. Both, within the same season, removed leaders who had each governed for well over a decade.

questions.q: What is the passage's central contrast between the Hungarian and Venezuelan transitions?
options: Both transitions happened through military intervention
Both transitions happened through free elections
One transition occurred through an election, the other through foreign military intervention
Neither transition actually resulted in a change of leadership
questions.explain: The passage's closing lines state this explicitly: 'One government fell to a ballot box... The other fell to foreign military force.'

questions.q: According to the passage, what was Peter Magyar's relationship to Viktor Orban before founding the Tisza Party?
options: He was a longtime opposition leader with no prior ties to Orban
He was an insider within Orban's own political circle before breaking away in 2023
He served as Hungary's President before Orban
He was a European Union official who had never worked in Hungarian domestic politics
questions.explain: The passage states Magyar was 'a former Orban-circle insider who broke away in 2023,' making him a defector from within Orban's own political network rather than a longstanding outside critic.

questions.q: Based on the passage, what evidence suggests that Venezuela's political transition remains incomplete despite Maduro's capture?
options: Chevron refused to do any business with the interim government
Observers noted that rebuilding courts, security services and the economy would take years, not months
Delcy Rodríguez immediately called new elections
The amnesty law freed every political prisoner in the country
questions.explain: The passage directly states that observers 'cautioned that rebuilding Venezuela's courts, security services and sanctions-battered economy would take years, not months,' and notes the amnesty law was 'limited,' not comprehensive.

questions.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: Fidesz won more parliamentary seats than the Tisza Party in the 2026 Hungarian election
Orban had governed Hungary continuously for sixteen years before his 2026 defeat
Maduro's government lasted a total of 13 years under chavismo
Chevron's agreement with Venezuela's interim government was signed before Maduro's capture
questions.explain: The passage states Orban's 'sixteen unbroken years in power.' Tisza (138 seats) outpaced Fidesz (55 seats); chavista rule spanned 27 years from 1999, not just Maduro's 13; and the Chevron deal was signed in April, three months after the January capture.

questions.q: The passage notes Venezuela's chavista government began under Hugo Chávez in 1999. What ideology, named after 19th-century independence leader Simón Bolívar, is closely associated with Chávez's political movement?
options: Peronism
Bolivarianism
Sandinismo
Zapatismo
questions.explain: This draws on background static knowledge: Chávez's movement is closely associated with Bolivarianism, named for Simón Bolívar, reflected in Venezuela's official name, the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela.
